prompt: A cheaper model was just released. Before switching, you need to know whether answer quality on your support questions drops.
tells: whether answer quality on your support questions drops
why: Run both models on a fixed test set and score them.
trap: Routing decides which model to use per request; you first need evidence of how they compare.

prompt: Every prompt tweak fixes one complaint and silently breaks something else that used to work.
tells: silently breaks something else that used to work
why: A regression test set run on every change catches breakage before it ships.
trap: More prompt tweaking without measurement just moves the bugs around.

prompt: You need to score 2,000 generated summaries for faithfulness each week, and no simple string check can tell good from bad.
why: Use an LLM judge with a rubric, calibrated against some human-graded examples.
trap: Batch inference is how you might run the judge cheaply, but the need is evaluation.

prompt: You changed the chunk size in your retrieval pipeline. Did answers get more accurate or less?
tells: Did answers get more accurate or less?
why: Measure retrieval and answer accuracy on a labeled question set before and after the change.
trap: It's about RAG, but the question is how to measure it.

prompt: Before launch, the team wants a fixed set of 300 real questions with approved answers to check every model or prompt change against.
tells: check every model or prompt change
why: That's a golden eval set, the foundation of regression testing for LLM apps.
trap: It's a test suite, not training data.

prompt: Prompt changes ship when two engineers say the new outputs "look better" on five examples.
why: Five examples and gut feel can't catch regressions; build a measured eval.
trap: The problem isn't the prompt; it's how changes are judged.

prompt: Offline scores for two prompts are tied. You want to know which one users actually prefer, measured by thumbs-up rate and follow-up questions.
why: Run an online eval (A/B test) on live traffic with user signals.
trap: Splitting traffic looks like routing, but the goal is measurement.

prompt: An LLM grader consistently prefers whichever of two answers is longer, regardless of accuracy.
tells: prefers whichever of two answers is longer
why: Calibrate the judge against human labels and control for length and position bias.
